doc.title: Ametria Dock interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 4, 2019

title: Preparing singers for clubs: set lists, fitting the room and band etiquette
summary: Dock coaches clients to choose songs suited to the venue, rehearse with the band, and give accompanists solo space when it is a real show.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom

blocks.x: Do singers have the responsibility regarding accompanists to make it more likely that they’re going to have a good experience. What is the singer’s responsibility?
Okay let me see what you mean.
Well let’s say you get invited to come up and sing. What would you want one of your students — how would they prepare for that?
Okay. How would they prepare to come up and sing —

Okay. So a lot I work on that for my clients. And so what we do is we sit down and we choose a set list for the types of songs. So there’s a lot of work that goes in. We have to think about where you’re going to perform, where you want to perform, so the types of clubs that you’re performing at. We have an Open Mic club that is more singer/ songwriter feel and so it’s more guitar and piano driven and so the types of songs that they sing at this particular club is more singer/songwriter as opposed to another club in the city that’s more like pop and R&B and soul. And so it’s about knowing where you fit, knowing — I wouldn’t take one of my soul songs and go to Eddie’s Attic in Atlanta, because it wouldn’t fit there. But I could go to Eddie’s Attic and I could sing a — who’s my favorite — a Joni Mitchell song. It would go over well there. So we pick a set list, we work on the songs, we choose instrumentals or if you have an accompanist that can come and we can work through the song, we work through the song and get them prepared. Most times if you’re doing live performances you want to make sure that you are rehearsing with the band and/or whomever will be playing with you.

Do your students learn about the etiquette of relating to accompanist or a band, like I’ve sung now you do a gesture to the piano player, you got it, that kind of thing, when to come back in on the bridge.

Yeah. So it varies from musician to musician. So there are some that are you know like I think it’s really cool when some of the artists that are well known that I work with, that they take a moment to allow the band, the musician, the pianist or guitar player a moment of soloing so when it’s that type of show you see more of that. When it’s a one-off where they’re just doing one song, most of the time you don’t see the singer giving the band member solos, unless at a club event, you know what I’m saying? Like if it’s an open mic. If it’s an open mic kind of show the singer is the focus. If it’s an actual show then everyone is the focus if that makes sense. In the culture in what I see, I see that happening a little bit more where the singer will kind of back off a little bit and then the pianist or the guitar player kind of just goes a little. So yeah.
